what_it_does: Near-memory processing (NMP) means adding simple compute units directly inside or very close to memory chips, so data does not have to travel far to be processed — this cuts energy and time for memory-heavy AI workloads. The problem is that each research group builds their simulator and compiler for one specific memory technology and one specific NMP chip design, making it impossible to fairly compare architectures or automatically find the best data placement and workload schedule across different designs. UniNDP proposes a single shared blueprint — a tree-shaped abstract description of any NMP hardware — and a matching instruction set that works across different memory technologies. It pairs this with a cycle-accurate simulator (one that tracks timing at the clock-cycle level) and a compiler that searches for the best way to divide AI workloads across the memory hierarchy, using the hardware blueprint's timing parameters to prune bad options quickly.
